title: Nonstandard Errors

cost.compute_notes: 2026-09-14 session: no new downloads (deposit already on disk from an earlier session, see artifacts/fincap/). Re-ran all 8 existing reanalysis scripts (f1,f2,f3,f4,f5,f6,f7,f8) fresh and folded their output into claims c1-c5, plus one new artifact entry (a4, the deposit itself) and one superseded quantity (the old tau-subtraction ratio). reanalysis/f3b_scale_confound.py, referenced by f3's own docstring and whose output JSON exists (artifacts/f3b_scale_confound.json), could not be found on disk this session -- its numbers are quoted as present-but-insufficient, not independently re-verified.

triggers: how large is researcher-induced dispersion compared to sampling error
does peer feedback reduce disagreement between analysts
does research quality reduce analyst dispersion
why use interquartile range instead of standard deviation across teams
do researchers know how much analysts disagree

claims.statement: Researcher-induced dispersion (the 'nonstandard error', defined as the interquartile range of estimates across research teams) is similar in magnitude to sampling error. For RT-H1, the NSE is 6.7 percentage points against a median across-team SE of 2.5%, whose Gaussian-implied IQR is 3.4.
claims.scope: 164 research teams, six pre-specified hypotheses, 17 years of EuroStoxx 50 index futures data supplied by Deutsche Boerse. Numbers quoted are for RT-H1 ('market efficiency has not changed over time'); the paper states dispersion is similar for the others.

quantities.name: researcher_dispersion_over_median_SE
quantities.baseline: the identical robust recipe on Breznau et al.'s CRI gives 1.72

quantities.name: single_extreme_reported_estimate
quantities.source: p. 2345 footnote 7; this one team moves the mean to 446.3% and the SD to 5817.5%

quantities.name: nse_over_median_se_direct
quantities.baseline: median across the 6 hypotheses, range 0.628-1.976. Supersedes researcher_dispersion_over_median_SE: that number used tau = sqrt((IQR/1.349)^2 - medianSE^2), which subtracts a sampling-variance term that does not exist here (all 164 teams analyse the SAME dataset, so there is no independent draw to net out) -- tau^2 comes out NEGATIVE on 3 of 6 hypotheses, the recipe telling us it does not apply. NSE/medianSE directly is the right comparison for a same-data design, and it says NSE and SE are close to equal in size, which matches Menkveld et al.'s own hedge more closely than the inflated 1.72 did.

quantities.name: overdispersion_var_ratio_stage1_two_sided
quantities.source: maria 2026, reanalysis/f1_overdispersion.py -- NARPS-style test: variance of each team's count of |t|>1.96 results (of 6) against a column-permutation null that fixes each hypothesis's own significant rate. z=20.5, p<0.0001. Present at all 4 stages (ratio falls monotonically 3.065 -> 2.232 as peer feedback proceeds, but stays far above 1 throughout).

quantities.name: between_team_variance_share_logSE_stage1
quantities.baseline: vs. 0.153 for the |estimate| itself, same rank-transform test
quantities.source: maria 2026, reanalysis/f3_trait_decomposition.py -- "reports a significant result" clusters by team predominantly through PRECISION (log SE), not through the estimate. Team-mean-rank(logSE) vs count-of-6-significant: rho=-0.801 (p=7e-38); team-mean-rank(|estimate|) vs same: rho=-0.292 (p=1.5e-4). A robustness variant using raw log-values instead of within-hypothesis ranks (f3b_scale_confound.py, script since lost -- see artifact note) gave icc-like shares 0.776 (logSE) vs 0.500 (log|estimate|): same qualitative conclusion, weaker margin. Not independently re-verified this session because the generating script is present-but-insufficient (see a5).

quantities.name: most_extreme_team_share_of_sum_of_squares
quantities.baseline: range across the 6 hypotheses: 0.280 (h6, stage4) to 0.994 (h1/h2/h4, both stages). 5 of 6 hypotheses have ONE team carrying 77-99% of the total across-team sum of squares.

our_assessment.why: [Independent reanalysis this session judged the claim would be 'accepted-narrower-scope' if read_depth allowed a non-unverified status -- it does not: read_depth is still skimmed (pages 2339-2350 of 52), and this schema correctly does not let assessment confidence outrun how much of the paper itself has been read, however solid the independent numbers are. Upgrade to read-full-text before revisiting this status.] VERIFIED AND EXTENDED from the deposit, 2026-09-14 (the paper text itself is still only pages 2339-2350; this is independent re-derivation from the raw team-level data, not a second read of their prose). The magnitude claim holds and is now on firmer footing: the quoted 1.72 used a subtraction recipe (tau^2 = NSE^2 - SE^2) that is invalid for a same-data design and returns a NEGATIVE tau^2 on half the hypotheses -- the direct ratio NSE/medianSE is close to 1 (median 1.050) instead, which if anything supports the "similar magnitude" claim more cleanly. The overdispersion itself is unambiguous (observed variance of per-team significance counts is 2.2x-3.1x a permutation null, p<0.0001, all 4 stages) and NEW here: it is driven mostly by teams clustering in PRECISION (between-team share of log(SE) variance 0.78) rather than in the point estimate itself (share 0.15-0.27) -- a mechanism the accessible pages do not discuss. And the whole corpus-level dispersion for most hypotheses is dominated by a single team (77-99% of the sum of squares), which is exactly the fat-tail behaviour the authors' own choice of IQR over SD anticipates (see c5) but is worth stating numerically: the '1.72' and '1.05' summary ratios both describe a distribution whose spread is mostly one observation.

claims.statement: Higher quality coincides with smaller dispersion: a one-SD increase in reproducibility reduces NSEs by 25.0% and a one-SD increase in peer-evaluator rating reduces them by 33.3%, while a one-SD increase in team quality raises them by 2.8%.
claims.scope: Quantile regressions on the IQR; the paper notes the team-quality effect is small in economic magnitude.

quantities.name: team_level_quality_cv_r2
quantities.source: maria 2026, reanalysis/f7_quality.py -- all three quality measures together predicting n_significant_of_6, 10-fold CV, negative R2 means worse than predicting the mean

quantities.name: team_level_resolving_rho_at_p05
quantities.source: maria 2026, reanalysis/f8_nse_over_se.py -- smallest |rho| reaching p<0.05 at n=164; f7's correlations are mostly below this, so the nulls are informative, not merely underpowered

our_assessment.why: [Independent reanalysis this session judged the claim would be 'disputed' if read_depth allowed a non-unverified status -- it does not: read_depth is still skimmed (pages 2339-2350 of 52), and this schema correctly does not let assessment confidence outrun how much of the paper itself has been read, however solid the independent numbers are. Upgrade to read-full-text before revisiting this status.] A DIFFERENT, natural operationalization of the same claim finds close to nothing at the team level, 2026-09-14. Menkveld et al.'s reported effect (a 1-SD increase in reproducibility/peer-rating cuts NSE 25-33%) is presumably a regression on an aggregate dispersion measure -- not accessible from the pages I have. The natural team-level test (does THIS team's quality predict how far ITS estimate sits from consensus, or its own precision, or how often it lands 'significant') finds weak, mostly non-significant rank correlations (|rho| 0.07-0.17, one borderline at p=0.033) and an out-of-fold R^2 from all three quality measures combined that is indistinguishable from a permuted-label control (-0.016 vs -0.017). At n=164 a real rho as small as 0.153 would already clear p<0.05 (f8), so this is not simply underpowered. Two readings are both live and I cannot adjudicate between them without Appendix B (not in the deposit): (a) the paper's effect is real but lives at a level of aggregation team-level rank correlation cannot see (e.g. it is about the SPREAD of quality-sorted subgroups, not an individual team's deviation), or (b) the reported quantile-regression coefficients are more fragile than the headline percentages suggest. Marked `disputed`, not `refuted`: their number is still the best available and mine does not directly contradict a quantity they published, it fails to reproduce the claim under a different, defensible operationalization.

claims.statement: Peer feedback reduces dispersion: no single stage does so significantly, but the four stages together reduce NSEs by 47.2% and interdecile ranges by 68.2%.
claims.scope: Staged design in which 34 peer evaluators each assessed about 10 papers in a single-blind process.

quantities.name: estimate_iqr_ratio_stage4_over_1_median
quantities.source: maria 2026, reanalysis/f5_t_divergence.py -- matches the reported -47.2% (0.528) within bootstrap noise, on the ESTIMATES

quantities.name: estimate_idr_ratio_stage4_over_1_median
quantities.source: maria 2026, reanalysis/f4_verify_quoted.py -- matches the reported -68.2% (0.318) within noise

quantities.name: tvalue_iqr_ratio_stage4_over_1_median
quantities.source: maria 2026, reanalysis/f5_t_divergence.py -- P(ratio>1)=0.990. The t-value, which is what actually decides 'significant or not', gets MORE dispersed across the four stages, not less

quantities.name: frac_teams_significant_h1_stage1_vs_4
quantities.source: maria 2026, reanalysis/f5_t_divergence.py -- fraction of teams with |t|>1.96, hypothesis 1; similar rises on h2 (28.7%->53.7%) and h3 (49.4%->86.6%)

our_assessment.why: [Independent reanalysis this session judged the claim would be 'accepted-narrower-scope' if read_depth allowed a non-unverified status -- it does not: read_depth is still skimmed (pages 2339-2350 of 52), and this schema correctly does not let assessment confidence outrun how much of the paper itself has been read, however solid the independent numbers are. Upgrade to read-full-text before revisiting this status.] VERIFIED on the estimates, 2026-09-14: the reported -47.2%/-68.2% falls are reproduced from the deposit within bootstrap noise (0.494 and 0.335 vs. reported 0.528 and 0.318). What is NOT in the accessible pages and is a genuine complication: the standard errors shrink even FASTER than the estimates converge (SE IQR ratio 0.173 vs. estimate IQR ratio 0.494), so the t-values -- which are what actually decide 'this team reports a significant result' -- get MORE dispersed across the four peer-feedback stages, not less (ratio 1.347, 95% CI [1.05, 1.67] excludes 1, P(ratio>1)=0.990), and the fraction of teams crossing the significance threshold rises sharply on most hypotheses (e.g. h1: 32.3% -> 61.6%). If this holds up against whatever Appendix B says (not in the deposit), the honest one-sentence summary is not 'peer feedback reduces disagreement' but 'peer feedback narrows point estimates while widening disagreement about the conclusion' -- a sharper and less comfortable claim than the one usually quoted from this paper. This is exactly the pattern I flagged as suspicious in NOTES.md before checking it (four individually-insignificant stages, significant together) -- it survives, but not in the direction I expected to find a problem in.

claims.statement: Research teams underestimate the dispersion in estimates across teams, measured in an incentivised belief survey.
claims.scope: Belief elicitation before results were revealed.

our_assessment.why: [Independent reanalysis this session judged the claim would be 'accepted-narrower-scope' if read_depth allowed a non-unverified status -- it does not: read_depth is still skimmed (pages 2339-2350 of 52), and this schema correctly does not let assessment confidence outrun how much of the paper itself has been read, however solid the independent numbers are. Upgrade to read-full-text before revisiting this status.] The incentivised belief data (984 forecasts) does NOT show a strong systematic underestimation at the median -- median prediction/realised-NSE is 0.912 (a mild underestimate) and forecasts split almost evenly around the realised NSE (49.7% below it), so 'teams underestimate dispersion' is at most a small median effect, not the dominant pattern in the data. The real, striking, and much cleaner finding: teams are near-perfectly CALIBRATED IN RANK across the six hypotheses -- which ones will disagree more -- when scored against the robust NSE (Spearman rho=1.000, n=6) but not against the raw, outlier-dominated SD (rho=0.429). That is a finding about relative calibration the accessible pages do not state this way (only the Summary of Findings was read; Appendix material on the belief survey, if any, is not in the deposit or the pages obtained). Individual point forecasts are noisy (only 29.9% land within a factor of 2 of the realised NSE), so 'underestimate' may be a true description of SOME hypotheses or SOME teams that does not survive aggregation to the median -- narrowed rather than accepted or refuted outright.

claims.statement: The distribution of estimates across analysts is heavy-tailed, which is why a robust dispersion measure is the right instrument: the authors adopt the IQR precisely because 'the distribution of the SD could exhibit fat tails and thus be prone to outliers'.
claims.scope: Statistical framework, p. 2344, plus footnote 7's single team reporting +74,491%.

quantities.name: interdecile_over_interquartile_ratio
quantities.baseline: Gaussian value 1.90; CRI model-level 2.79; CRI team-level 2.08

quantities.name: idr_over_iqr_stage1
quantities.baseline: Gaussian reference 1.90 (stable across n); range across 6 hypotheses 3.07-11.59 (h6)
quantities.source: maria 2026, reanalysis/f4_verify_quoted.py -- re-verifies the quoted NOTES.md number exactly

quantities.name: most_extreme_team_share_of_sum_of_squares_range
quantities.source: maria 2026, reanalysis/f4_verify_quoted.py -- one team, out of 164, carrying this share of the total across-team sum of squares on 5 of 6 hypotheses

our_assessment.why: [Independent reanalysis this session judged the claim would be 'accepted' if read_depth allowed a non-unverified status -- it does not: read_depth is still skimmed (pages 2339-2350 of 52), and this schema correctly does not let assessment confidence outrun how much of the paper itself has been read, however solid the independent numbers are. Upgrade to read-full-text before revisiting this status.] STRONGLY CONFIRMED AND EXTENDED, 2026-09-14, from the full team-level deposit rather than the one footnoted number available in 2026-08-12: on 5 of 6 hypotheses a SINGLE team out of 164 carries 77-99% of the entire across-team sum of squares. This is not a mild departure from Gaussian that IQR modestly improves on -- it is a distribution whose spread is nearly one observation, which makes IDR/IQR itself (4.07 vs the Gaussian-stable reference 1.90) an undersell of how extreme the tail is, since IDR/IQR only sees the 10th/90th percentiles and the one dominant team can sit further out than that. The authors' choice of a robust measure is vindicated more strongly than their own quoted footnote (one team at +74,491%) by itself suggests.

relations.why: Independently, in a different field, with 164 teams instead of 71 and a robust rather than a variance-based instrument: researcher-induced dispersion is of the same order as sampling error, and the estimate distribution is heavy-tailed. Our reanalysis reached both by fighting a variance decomposition that was the wrong tool; they simply chose the right tool at the design stage.

Their quality-versus-dispersion associations at n = 164 are of a size Breznau et al.'s n = 71 design could not have detected. The sociology null and the finance effect are compatible; reading the null as 'expertise does not matter' is not.

Menkveld et al. cite Breznau et al. as prior art (p. 2347, and again in footnote 1 on translating conceptual into empirical research questions). The citation runs finance -> sociology; nothing runs the other way, and neither cites the LLM-monoculture literature.

PROPOSED BY kb.py suggest, accepted on the method rather than the substance: Menkveld et al. adopt the interquartile range as the dispersion measure precisely because the cross-analyst distribution is heavy-tailed, and this record uses the same robust dispersion logic on a within-sample rather than a cross-analyst distribution.

Reciprocal. The choice of a dispersion measure is treated as technical in both literatures; here it reverses the conclusion, which argues that dispersion measures deserve the scrutiny given to point estimates.

Menkveld's standard/nonstandard error split is the right vocabulary for NARPS: the team random intercept (sigma 0.97-1.32 on the logit scale) is a nonstandard error in the CONCLUSION, and NARPS's own voxelwise tau of 1.13-1.85 is one in the ESTIMATE, against a sampling SD of at least 1.0.
